## Using the knowledge base

Source: https://aerotec-atlas.github.io/knowledge_base/using-the-knowledge-base/

This site is the ATLAS knowledge base. It holds explanations, project notes,
mission records, and references. Pages are written so a person can read them
and an AI agent can use them as context.

For how the site works as shared team memory and AI context, see
[Team memory and AI wiki](team-memory.md).

## Read a page

- Use the left sidebar to move between areas and pages. The right sidebar lists
  the sections on the current page.
- Use search to find a term, command, or topic.
- Check the frontmatter before relying on a detail:
    - `status: draft` means the content is not fully verified.
    - `status: verified` means the commands or content were checked.
    - `status: stale` means the page may no longer match the code.
    - `status: deprecated` means the page is kept for history.
- Check `applies_to` for the commit or version the page was checked against.
- Follow the source links before copying a command or parameter.

## Add or edit a page

### 1. Choose the page type

| Type | Use it for | Suggested sections |
|---|---|---|
| Explanation | How something works, why a choice was made, or how the pieces fit together. | Context, How it works, Trade-offs, Source |
| Project | A new project, initiative, or workstream. | Goal, Scope, Owner, Status, Next steps, Links |
| Mission | A specific flight, test, demo, or simulation mission. | Objective, Setup, Procedure, Results, Open issues |
| How-to | A repeatable task with commands or steps. | Before you start, Steps, Verify, Troubleshoot |
| Reference | Commands, parameters, ports, or other lookup material. | Tables, Notes, Source |

If a page fits more than one type, pick the one that answers the reader's main
question and link to the others instead of duplicating content.

### 2. Create the file

Create a Markdown file under `docs/`:

```text
docs/new-project.md
docs/control-mission-planning/new-mission.md
```

Use lowercase words separated by hyphens. Start every page with frontmatter:

```yaml
---
title: Short page title
description: One sentence that explains what the page is for.
owner: Control & Mission Planning
status: draft
last_reviewed: 2026-10-25
applies_to: atlas_ws@<commit>   # optional
tags: [simulation, mavros]
---
```

Use `status: draft` until someone actually runs the commands or checks the
content. Do not mark a page `verified` from memory.

### 3. Add it to the navigation

Add the page to `nav` in `mkdocs.yml`:

```yaml
nav:
  - Home: index.md
  - Using the knowledge base: using-the-knowledge-base.md
  - Team memory and AI wiki: team-memory.md
  - Areas:
      - Control & Mission Planning:
          - control-mission-planning/index.md
          - Multi-drone: control-mission-planning/multi-drone.md
          - New mission: control-mission-planning/new-mission.md
```

A page that is not in `nav` is hard to find. If you create a new area, also add
an `index.md` for that area.

### 4. Link it from the home page or area index

Add a link from `docs/index.md` if the page is a starting point. Otherwise, link
it from the area index:

```markdown
- [New mission](control-mission-planning/new-mission.md)
```

Keep links relative to the page that contains them. If you move a page, update
the links that point to it.

### 5. Run the checks

```bash
bash scripts/check.sh
```

The script regenerates `docs/llms.txt` and `docs/llms-full.txt`, then runs a
strict Zensical build. Broken navigation entries, broken internal links, and
missing anchors fail the build.

Do not commit `site/` or `.venv/`.

## Appendix: How AI should create a page

An AI agent with the repository open can do the first draft, update `nav`, and
run the checks. Give it a prompt like this:

```text
Add a new <explanation | project | mission | how-to | reference> page to the ATLAS knowledge base.

Topic: <topic>
Owner: <owner>
Goal: <what the reader should understand or be able to do>
Sources: <atlas_ws paths, logs, links, or existing pages>
Status: draft

Follow AGENTS.md and docs/using-the-knowledge-base.md.

1. Choose the right page type and a short filename under docs/.
2. Create the page with complete frontmatter.
3. Add it to nav in mkdocs.yml and link it from docs/index.md or the relevant area index.
4. Run bash scripts/check.sh.
5. Report the files changed and anything you could not verify.

Do not invent commands, ports, parameters, or results. If a fact is missing from the sources, write "not verified" or leave a clear TODO. Do not mark the page verified.
```

The agent should read `AGENTS.md`, the pages named in the prompt, and the source
files before writing. Code wins over memory and older notes. Ask for a small
diff, not a rewrite of the site.

Review the result:

- Does the page answer the question from the prompt?
- Are commands, ports, parameters, and results backed by a source?
- Does the page say what was not tested?
- Is it in the right area and in `nav`?
- Does the home page or area index link to it?
- Does `bash scripts/check.sh` pass?
- Did the agent avoid secrets, personal data, and unrelated changes?

## Examples

### Explanation page

```markdown
---
title: How the telemetry link works
description: The path from the autopilot to the ground station.
owner: Control & Mission Planning
status: draft
last_reviewed: 2026-10-25
tags: [telemetry, mavlink]
---

# How the telemetry link works

## Context

What problem this link solves and where it sits in the system.

## How it works

The flow, the endpoints, and the protocols involved.

## Trade-offs

What is simple, what is fragile, and what was not tested.

## Source

- `atlas_ws/path/to/the/source`
```

### New project page

```markdown
---
title: Project name
description: What the project is trying to achieve.
owner: Project owner
status: draft
last_reviewed: 2026-10-25
tags: [project]
---

# Project name

## Goal

The outcome the project should produce.

## Scope

What is included and what is deliberately out of scope.

## Owner and status

Who owns it, who is helping, and the current state.

## Next steps

- [ ] First concrete step.
- [ ] Second concrete step.

## Links

- Repository, issue, design document, or source file.
```

### Mission page

```markdown
---
title: Mission name
description: What this mission is meant to demonstrate.
owner: Mission owner
status: draft
last_reviewed: 2026-10-25
applies_to: atlas_ws@<commit>
tags: [mission]
---

# Mission name

## Objective

What the vehicle should do and what counts as success.

## Setup

Vehicle, firmware, airframe, location, and simulation or flight environment.

## Procedure

The steps to run the mission.

## Results

What happened. Include the date and the commit or configuration used.

## Open issues

What failed, what is uncertain, and what needs a follow-up.

## Links

- Source files, logs, videos, or related pages.
```

## Before you publish

- Remove placeholders such as `<commit>` and `Project owner`.
- Say what was not tested.
- Do not include credentials, tokens, personal data, or sensitive operational
  details.
- Run `bash scripts/check.sh` again after the final edit.

---

## Team memory and AI wiki

Source: https://aerotec-atlas.github.io/knowledge_base/team-memory/

This site is not only documentation. It is the team's shared memory: what was
tried, what worked, what is still open, and where the source lives. It is also
the context an AI agent reads before it helps with code, missions, or planning.

For the mechanics of adding or editing a page, see
[Using the knowledge base](using-the-knowledge-base.md).

## What this gives the team

- A single place for decisions and the reasons behind them.
- A starting point for someone joining a project or area.
- A record of missions, tests, and experiments that is easier to find than a
  chat history.
- Context for AI agents, so they do not start from zero on every task.
- A place to keep links to source, logs, and issues without copying everything.

## What belongs here

| Content | Example |
|---|---|
| Explanation | How a subsystem works, or why a design was chosen. |
| Project | Goal, scope, owner, status, next steps, and links. |
| Mission | Objective, setup, procedure, results, and open issues. |
| How-to | A task that someone needs to repeat. |
| Reference | Commands, parameters, ports, or configuration. |
| Decision record | What was decided, when, by whom, and what was rejected. |

A page can start small. Three clear paragraphs with a source link are more
useful than a long page with no owner and no verification.

## Write for memory, not for a meeting

- One concept per page. Split pages that grow past a few screens.
- Start with the question the page answers.
- Link the source instead of copying large code blocks.
- Record the date, commit, and what was not tested.
- Use explicit nouns. Avoid ambiguous “it” and “this”.
- Give every page an owner and a review date.
- Keep a page `draft` until someone checks it.

## If you are developing something

Create a project page before the work becomes hard to reconstruct. Start with:

```markdown
## Goal

## Scope

## Owner and status

## Next steps

## Links
```

As the work moves, add mission pages, experiment notes, and decisions to the
project page. At the end, record the result, what failed, and what still needs a
follow-up. The project page becomes the memory of the work, not a status report
that disappears after the sprint.

## How AI uses this site

- `AGENTS.md` contains the rules an agent must follow.
- `docs/llms.txt` is the compact index of pages.
- `docs/llms-full.txt` is every page concatenated in navigation order.
- The `nav` in `mkdocs.yml` defines the reading order.

An AI agent should read the relevant page and its linked source. The code wins
over the page when they disagree. The agent should not invent commands, ports,
parameters, or results, and it should say what it could not verify.

### Ask AI to use the knowledge base

Use a prompt like this when you want an answer from the site:

```text
Read AGENTS.md and the pages about <topic>. Answer <question>.
Cite the page or source file for each claim. If the answer is not in the
knowledge base, say so and check the code.
```

Use a prompt like this when the memory needs to change:

```text
Read <page> and <source>. Update the page to match the current code.
Keep status: draft until I verify it. Record the commit and what was not tested.
Do not change unrelated pages.
```

### Ask AI to review the memory

An agent can also look for problems across the site:

```text
Review the pages under <area>. Find stale links, claims without a source,
commands that no longer match the code, and pages that should be marked stale.
Do not rewrite the pages. List the problems and the source you checked.
```

## What not to put here

- Credentials, tokens, personal data, or sensitive operational details.
- Large code blocks, raw logs, or datasets. Link to them instead.
- Guesses presented as facts.
- Meeting transcripts without a short summary.
- Pages without an owner or a review date.

## Keep it current

- Update `last_reviewed` when you review a page.
- Move `status` from `draft` to `verified` only after checking the content.
- Mark a page `stale` when the code has moved on.
- Keep `deprecated` pages for history instead of deleting them.
- When a page is renamed, update the links and the navigation.

The knowledge base is useful only while the team trusts it. A small, current
page with a clear source is better than a complete page that nobody has checked.

## Control & Mission Planning

Source: https://aerotec-atlas.github.io/knowledge_base/control-mission-planning/

This area covers how ATLAS vehicles are told what to do.

- [Multi-drone simulation](multi-drone.md)

---

## Control & Mission Planning / Multi-drone simulation

Source: https://aerotec-atlas.github.io/knowledge_base/control-mission-planning/multi-drone/

`ap-multi` runs two or more ArduCopter vehicles in **one Gazebo world**. Each
vehicle has its own SITL process, its own MAVROS namespace, and its own mission
agent. The demo is also a communication test: drone 1 flies a square, then sends
drone 2 a waypoint; drone 2 waits in a GUIDED hold until it receives it.

!!! info "What this page covers"
    The topology, the namespace/port scheme, how the world is generated, how to
    launch the demo, the agent state machine, the inter-drone topics, and the
    known limitations.

## Topology

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    subgraph GZ["Gazebo Harmonic — one world"]
        D1["drone1 / iris_ap1<br/>fdm_port_in 9002"]
        D2["drone2 / iris_ap2<br/>fdm_port_in 9012"]
    end

    D1 -->|"UDP JSON"| S1["arducopter<br/>instance 0 · sysid 1"]
    D2 -->|"UDP JSON"| S2["arducopter<br/>instance 1 · sysid 2"]

    S1 -->|"TCP 5760"| M1["MAVROS<br/>/drone1/mavros"]
    S2 -->|"TCP 5770"| M2["MAVROS<br/>/drone2/mavros"]

    M1 --> A1["drone_agent<br/>__ns=/drone1"]
    M2 --> A2["drone_agent<br/>__ns=/drone2"]

    A1 -->|"/drone2/cmd/waypoint"| A2
    A2 -->|"/drone2/status"| A1
```

There are three independent channels per drone:

1. **Physics**: the Gazebo model sends JSON/UDP to ArduPilot SITL on its
   `fdm_port_in` port.
2. **MAVLink**: SITL exposes TCP `5760 + 10·(K−1)`, and MAVROS connects to it.
3. **ROS 2**: MAVROS and the agent share a namespace, so the same agent code
   produces `/droneK/...` topics for every vehicle.

## Ports and IDs

| Drone | Gazebo FDM port | SITL instance | MAVLink `sysid` | SITL TCP | MAVROS namespace |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 9002 | 0 | 1 | 5760 | `/drone1` |
| 2 | 9012 | 1 | 2 | 5770 | `/drone2` |
| K | `9002 + 10(K−1)` | `K−1` | `K` | `5760 + 10(K−1)` | `/droneK` |

## Why namespaces

You do not write a separate mission node for each drone. You write one node that
uses **relative** ROS names:

```python
'mavros/state'
'mavros/local_position/pose'
'mavros/setpoint_position/local'
'cmd/waypoint'
'status'
```

Then you start the same node once per drone:

```bash
python3 docs/multi_missoes/drone_agent.py --ros-args -r __ns:=/drone1
python3 docs/multi_missoes/drone_agent.py --ros-args -r __ns:=/drone2
```

ROS 2 resolves every relative name under the node namespace. MAVROS is launched
with the matching namespace:

```bash
ros2 launch mavros apm.launch ... namespace:=drone1
ros2 launch mavros apm.launch ... namespace:=drone2
```

The result is two complete topic trees:

```text
/drone1/mavros/state
/drone1/mavros/local_position/pose
/drone1/mavros/setpoint_position/local
/drone1/status
/drone1/cmd/waypoint

/drone2/mavros/state
/drone2/mavros/local_position/pose
/drone2/mavros/setpoint_position/local
/drone2/status
/drone2/cmd/waypoint
```

!!! warning "Namespace trap"
    Use `namespace:=drone1`, not `namespace:=drone1/mavros`. The second form
    produces `/drone1/mavros/mavros/...`.

## The world is generated, not spawned

`ap-multi` does not call `ros_gz_sim create` at runtime. Runtime spawning caused
timeouts and made Gazebo and the launch process depend on a shared `/tmp`. Instead
the script generates the world before starting anything:

1. Copy the upstream `iris_with_ardupilot` model for each drone.
2. Rename each copy (`iris_ap1`, `iris_ap2`, …) and change its `fdm_port_in`
   (`9002`, `9012`, …).
3. Copy `iris_runway.sdf`, rename the world, and insert all drone models at
   `x = (K−1) · SPACING`.
4. Remove the Gazebo sensors/render plugin. The demo has no cameras, and the
   render system only costs CPU.
5. Write `.multi_sim/worlds/multi_iris_runway.sdf`.

The generated files live under `.multi_sim/` and are not committed.

## Launch it

Inside the container (rebuild the image first if the scripts changed):

```bash
cd ~/git_projects/atlas_ws/docker
xhost +local:docker
docker compose run --rm dev ap-multi demo
```

If the image predates the scripts, run the current file directly:

```bash
docker compose run --rm dev bash /home/ros/atlas_ws/docker/scripts/ap-multi demo
```

| Command | What it does |
|---|---|
| `ap-multi demo` | Gazebo + 2 SITLs + 2 MAVROS + 2 agents. The default demo. |
| `ap-multi demo 3` | Same with 3 drones (drone 3 only waits; see limitations). |
| `ap-multi` | Gazebo + 2 SITLs + 2 MAVROS, no agents. |
| `ap-multi 3` | Same with 3 drones. |
| `ap-multi gen 2` | Only generate the world and models. |
| `ap-multi down` | Kill the tmux session and all simulation processes. |

Environment variables:

| Variable | Default | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| `GUI=1` | off | Open the Gazebo window (`gz sim -g`). |
| `SPEEDUP` | `1` | SITL speed multiplier. |
| `SPACING` | `3` | Distance between drones on the X axis, in metres. |
| `WIPE=1` | off | Delete saved SITL parameters (`-w`). |
| `GCS=1` | off | Forward MAVLink to QGroundControl on UDP 14550. Not verified. |
| `NO_TMUX=1` | off | Run in the background; logs go to `.multi_sim/logs/`. |
| `SETTLE` | `20` | Seconds between Gazebo → SITL and SITL → MAVROS. Use 40 on a slow PC. |

The tmux session has three windows: `sim` (Gazebo + SITLs), `mavros` (both MAVROS
instances), and `agents` (one `drone_agent.py` per drone). With `GUI=1` there is a
fourth `gui` window. Switch windows with `Ctrl-b n` / `Ctrl-b p`; detach with
`Ctrl-b d`; reattach with `tmux attach -t multi`.

## What happens in the demo

| Time | Event |
|---|---|
| T+0 | Gazebo starts with both drones already in the world. |
| T+`SETTLE` | Both SITL processes start. |
| A few seconds later | Both MAVROS instances start (`SETTLE + 8` in the tmux path). |
| After another short delay | The agents start (`SETTLE + 12` in the tmux path; `NO_TMUX` waits another `SETTLE`). Drone 2 is told to wait; drone 1 gets the square. |
| Drone 1 takeoff | GUIDED → arm → takeoff to 5 m. |
| Drone 1 mission | `(0,0,5)` → `(10,0,5)` → `(10,10,5)` → `(0,10,5)`. |
| Drone 1 at WP 2 | Sends `(3,12,8)` to `/drone2/cmd/waypoint` and repeats at 1 Hz until drone 2 confirms. |
| Drone 2 | Takes off to 8 m, holds position, receives the waypoint, flies to `(3,12,8)`, reports `ARRIVED`, waits 5 s, lands. |
| Drone 1 end | Lands after the last waypoint. |

The script starts the waiting drone first, but the 1 Hz handshake makes the start
order irrelevant.

## Flight logic

`drone_agent.py` is a state machine:

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> WAIT_FCU
    WAIT_FCU --> GUIDED: connected + pose
    GUIDED --> ARM: mode is GUIDED
    ARM --> TAKEOFF: armed
    TAKEOFF --> MISSION: altitude reached and waypoints exist
    TAKEOFF --> LOITER: wait_for_cmd or no waypoints
    MISSION --> LAND: last waypoint and land_at_end
    MISSION --> LOITER: last waypoint
    LOITER --> GOTO_CMD: /cmd/waypoint received
    GOTO_CMD --> ARRIVED: within tolerance
    ARRIVED --> LAND: land_at_end after land_delay_s
    LAND --> [*]
```

Key details:

- **GUIDED is the backbone.** The "loiter" is not ArduCopter LOITER mode. It is
  GUIDED with a constant position setpoint.
- **Stream rates are requested automatically.** MAVROS connects but does not
  publish `local_position/pose` until ArduPilot is asked to send the messages.
  The agent calls `mavros/set_stream_rate` while waiting for the FCU.
- **Sensor QoS is required.** `local_position/pose` is BEST_EFFORT; the agent
  subscribes with `qos_profile_sensor_data`.
- **Takeoff uses `CommandTOL`.** The agent then switches to position setpoints.
- **Arming retries.** A failed arm (EKF/GPS not ready) is retried until it works.

## Communication contract

| Topic | Type | Direction | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `/droneK/cmd/waypoint` | `geometry_msgs/PoseStamped` | peer → drone K | Target in the world frame (ENU). |
| `/droneK/status` | `std_msgs/String` | drone K → peers | Current phase, published at 1 Hz. |

Status values include `LOITER`, `MISSION wp=2/4`, `GOTO_CMD`, `ARRIVED`, and
`LAND`. The sender repeats the waypoint at 1 Hz until it sees `GOTO_CMD` or
`ARRIVED` in the peer's status.

Test the communication without flying the full demo:

```bash
ros2 topic pub -t 3 -r 1 /drone2/cmd/waypoint geometry_msgs/msg/PoseStamped \
  "{pose: {position: {x: 8.0, y: 0.0, z: 8.0}}}"
ros2 topic echo /drone2/status
```

## Frames and coordinates

In this setup, every SITL starts from the same GPS origin, so each drone's MAVROS
local frame coincides with the Gazebo world frame. A drone spawned at `x=3`
appears at `pose_local=(3.0, 0.0)`. That is why `origin_x` and `origin_y` are
`0.0` and the waypoints are plain world coordinates.

If you give each drone a different home, subtract its home position:

```text
local = world − home
```

The `frame_id` fields (`map` for setpoints, `world` for peer messages) are
informational; the numbers are already in the same world frame.

## Collision avoidance

Drone K flies at `5 + 3·(K−1)` metres:

| Drone | Altitude |
|---|---|
| 1 | 5 m |
| 2 | 8 m |
| 3 | 11 m |

This is deliberately simple. Drone 1's square passes through the ground point
where drone 2 holds position; at the same altitude, the two collided in testing.
The separation is not a general collision-avoidance system.

## Manual debugging

One terminal per piece, all inside the same container:

```bash
# 1. Generate only
ap-multi gen 2

# 2. Gazebo (server)
gz sim -s -r -v3 /home/ros/atlas_ws/.multi_sim/worlds/multi_iris_runway.sdf

# 3. One SITL per drone (run each in its own directory)
cd /tmp && arducopter --model json --speedup 1 --slave 0 \
  --sim-address=127.0.0.1 --instance 0 --sysid 1 \
  --defaults "$ARDUPILOT_HOME"/Tools/autotest/default_params/copter.parm,"$ARDUPILOT_HOME"/Tools/autotest/default_params/gazebo-iris.parm

# 4. One MAVROS per drone
ros2 launch mavros apm.launch fcu_url:=tcp://127.0.0.1:5760 tgt_system:=1 namespace:=drone1
ros2 launch mavros apm.launch fcu_url:=tcp://127.0.0.1:5770 tgt_system:=2 namespace:=drone2

# 5. Agents
python3 docs/multi_missoes/drone_agent.py --ros-args -r __ns:=/drone2 \
  -p takeoff_alt:=8.0 -p wait_for_cmd:=true
python3 docs/multi_missoes/drone_agent.py --ros-args -r __ns:=/drone1 \
  -p takeoff_alt:=5.0 \
  -p waypoints:="0,0,5;10,0,5;10,10,5;0,10,5" \
  -p peer_ns:=/drone2 -p notify_at_wp:=2 -p notify_wp:="3,12,8"
```

Useful checks:

```bash
ros2 topic list | grep mavros
ros2 topic echo /drone1/mavros/state --once
ros2 topic echo /drone2/status
ros2 service call /drone1/mavros/set_stream_rate mavros_msgs/srv/StreamRate \
  "{stream_id: 0, message_rate: 10, on_off: true}"
```

## Common errors

| Symptom | Cause | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| `arducopter` exits and prints `Options:` | `--use_sim_time` only exists when ArduPilot is built with DDS. | Use `ap-multi` (it does not pass the option), or build with `--enable-DDS`. |
| Gazebo: `Error finding file [/tmp/....yaml]` | Gazebo and the launch process are in different containers, so `/tmp` is not shared. | Run everything in the same container. |
| `Found additional publishers on /stats`, nothing works | Two Gazebo servers are running. | `ap-multi down`; remove leftover dev containers. |
| `create: request timed out` | The world was not ready, or the spawn service is not reachable. | `ap-multi` pre-generates the world; if it persists, `export GZ_IP=127.0.0.1`. |
| `package 'micro_ros_agent' not found` | `multiagent.launch.py` requires micro-ROS. | Do not use that launch; `ap-multi` does not need it. |
| Agent stuck in `WAIT_FCU`, `connected: true` | No stream rates, so no `local_position/pose`. | The agent requests them; manually call `set_stream_rate` if needed. |
| `InvalidTopicName: '//drone2/cmd/waypoint'` | `peer_ns:=/drone2` with a leading slash. | The agent strips the slash; update if you use an old version. |
| Topics at `/drone1/mavros/mavros/...` | `namespace:=drone1/mavros` in `apm.launch`. | Use `namespace:=drone1`. |
| MAVROS aborts: `egm96-5.pgm` not readable | Missing GeographicLib geoid dataset. | Run `install_geographiclib_datasets.sh`; the image should include it. |
| Parameter timeouts in MAVROS | Two MAVROS instances connected to the same SITL port. | One MAVROS per drone; `ap-multi down` and retry. |
| One drone falls and disarms | Both drones at the same altitude; the square crosses the hold point. | Separate altitudes (`5 + 3·(K−1)`). |
| `controller has reset`, `Time jump detected` in a loop | The PC is overloaded and SITL loses sync with Gazebo. | `SETTLE=40`, close the GUI, fewer drones, `WIPE=1`. |
| `bash: ap-multi: Permission denied` | Script is not executable, or the image is old. | `bash …/ap-multi demo` or rebuild the image. |
| `'arducopter' is not in PATH` | SITL was not built. | `atlas-build --packages-select ardupilot_sitl` or `ap-check`. |
| SITL stays in `Waiting for connection` | Normal until MAVROS connects; start order matters. | Start Gazebo first, then SITL, then MAVROS. |

## Limitations

- `ap-multi` is a **two-drone demo**, not a swarm scheduler. With `N > 2`, only
  drone 1 sends a waypoint to drone 2; the other drones hold position and, because
  `wait_for_cmd=true`, never receive an `ARRIVED` and therefore never land.
- The demo has **no real perception or collision avoidance**. Altitude separation
  is a manual rule.
- `GCS=1` and the Gazebo GUI path were not fully verified in the `atlas-sim:humble`
  container according to the source checklist.
- Everything runs in one container. That avoids `/tmp` and ROS discovery problems,
  but there is no process isolation.
- The world generator expects the current upstream `iris_with_ardupilot` model
  strings. If upstream changes the model name or `fdm_port_in`, `ap-multi` stops
  with a clear error instead of silently producing a broken world.

## Source files

- `docker/scripts/ap-multi` — world generation, SITL/MAVROS/agent orchestration.
- `docs/multi_missoes/drone_agent.py` — the per-drone state machine.
- `docs/multi_missoes/README.md` — the original Portuguese notes and test log.
- `docker/scripts/ap-help` — the `multi` section of the quick manual.
